Now before anyone gets all in a tizzy, here's what a defective autopsy actually means:

Negative autopsy is one, when gross and histopathological examination, toxological, microbiological, serological and other laboratory examinations fail to reveal a cause of death. The term "negative autopsy" is used in a wrong sense by several books, wehich tend to include so called "defective autopsies" within this term. Whenever a well-established [post-mortem] procedure, technique or ancillary investigation is not done, be it due to ignorance, lack of training or due to non-availability of resources, etc, it is a defective autopsy. ... There are thus four kinds of autopsies:

(i) Normal autopsy - cause is apparent from gross examination.
(ii) Defective autopsy - cause was ascertainable, but was not ascertained due to some constraint on the part of the doctor, hospital, facilities, etc.
(iii) Obscure autopsy - gross findings are minimal, indecisive, or obscure as in adrenal insufficiency, anesthetic overdose, mexedema, rare plant poisons, thyrotoxicosis etc. Subsequent examinations such as histology, microbiology, serology or toxicology reports establish the diagnosis.
(iv) Negative autopsy - Cause is not clear from gross as well as subsequent examinations. Some pathologists merge obscure autopsies with normal autopsies to avoid confusion.

Causes of defective autopsy: lack of competence or inadequate training of doctor. (The examiner and/or coroner missed something significant).

Citation: APC Textbook of Forensic Medicine and Toxicology, p. 169 Link: https://books.google.com/books?id=zbjiCQAAQBAJ&lpg=PA169&ots=TbrVaalljh&dq=%22defective%22%20autopsy%20-%22sandra%20bland%22&pg=PA169#v=onepage&q=%22defective%22%20autopsy%20-%22sandra%20bland%22&f=false
